reference_opening.argument: This video is non-scam content because it presents a Domino's-themed game tied to receiving a free pizza, consistent with an ordinary promotional or branded-game context. The later screens show routine ordering, points history, and rewards FAQs, which provide context for the promotion without establishing deception or a harmful transaction mechanism. The records do not verify the offer's eligibility rules, fulfillment, or official status.

citations.quote: HOW TO GET A FREE DOMINOS PIZZA!
You only have to play a game designed by dominos to get a FREE pizza!

opening.argument: The central promise is a free pizza, and it is explicitly conditioned on viewer participation: the title presents a method for getting one, while the description says viewers only have to play a Domino's-designed game. That is a low-barrier reward linked to an action, not merely a discussion of pizza or gaming. The video therefore solicits participation by presenting the game as the route to the reward. The available evidence does not establish the eligibility rules, how completion is verified, or how the promised pizza is actually delivered.

citations.quote: HOW TO GET A FREE DOMINOS PIZZA!
You only have to play a game designed by dominos to get a FREE pizza!

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling this an ordinary branded game does not remove the solicitation: the description expressly links playing the game to receiving a free pizza. The ordering and rewards screens show a branded app context, but they do not establish that the advertised game reward is genuine, available to this viewer, or fulfilled as represented. Routine app navigation is not proof of the specific offer.

citations.quote: You only have to play a game designed by dominos to get a FREE pizza!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The quoted material shows only a promotional claim and a game-related condition; it does not show a deceptive claim flow, payment demand, sensitive-data request, or failure to deliver. The app screens provide ordinary ordering and rewards context, while the claim that the game leads to a pizza remains consistent with a promotion.

citations.quote: HOW TO GET A FREE DOMINOS PIZZA!
You only have to play a game designed by dominos to get a FREE pizza!

opening.argument: The strongest warning sign is the unusually easy return: a viewer is told that merely playing a six-stage game can produce a free pizza. The offer is framed as a simple, attractive reward rather than a normal purchase, and the video supplies no visible qualification or fulfillment terms for the headline promise. The rewards history screen also shows points, qualifying orders, expiration, and an order threshold, indicating that rewards are conditional and administratively constrained. Taken together, the easy headline reward and incomplete conditions warrant treating the promotion as potentially deceptive rather than assuming the promise is straightforward.

citations.quote: HOW TO GET A FREE DOMINOS PIZZA!

rebuttal.rebuttal: The existence of a points history and rewards FAQ does not validate the headline offer; it may instead show that eligibility and expiration conditions matter. The defense identifies ordinary-looking screens, but ordinary design is not evidence that the free-pizza promise is available on the terms implied. The absence of a visible payment demand does not resolve whether the reward claim is misleading.

citations.quote: HOW TO GET A FREE DOMINOS PIZZA!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The risk argument relies on treating a free promotional reward as inherently suspicious. The evidence does not show urgency, an external claim link, a deposit, or a false testimonial. The rewards screen instead displays ordinary qualification and expiration information, so the quoted easy-reward language does not establish deception or a scam mechanism.

citations.quote: You only have to play a game designed by dominos to get a FREE pizza!

opening.argument: Although the footage includes gameplay, its practical role is promotional: the title is phrased as a direct guide to obtaining a free pizza, and the description tells viewers that playing the branded game is sufficient. The later app view displays pizza ordering and reward-related navigation, reinforcing a path from attention to participation in the brand's ecosystem. This is therefore not neutral gameplay coverage. It steers viewers toward an attractive reward while leaving the operative terms of the offer unverified.

citations.quote: HOW TO GET A FREE DOMINOS PIZZA!
You only have to play a game designed by dominos to get a FREE pizza!

rebuttal.rebuttal: The defense's label of ordinary promotion concedes the key point that the content steers viewers toward participation. A game can be promotional and still make an unsupported or misleading reward promise. The pizza-ordering screen establishes branding and commerce context, but does not prove that playing this game actually earns the advertised free pizza.

citations.quote: HOW TO GET A FREE DOMINOS PIZZA!

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Promotional steering is not the same as scamming. The title and description identify a branded game and a reward, but they do not show that viewers are sent to an unsafe destination or asked for money or sensitive information. The ordering and rewards screens are consistent with ordinary brand promotion, and the material does not prove the reward is false.
